result: SAA solubilizes POPC multilamellar vesicles (MLV) into small HDL-sized particles (~8 nm) that serve as excellent substrates for sPLA2 hydrolysis, whereas POPC MLV alone are not hydrolyzed by sPLA2. This ability distinguishes SAA from other HDL proteins like apoA-I and apoA-II.
evaluation: Claims C16-C21 provide converging experimental evidence from turbidity measurements (C16, C17), non-denaturing PAGE (C17), enzymatic assays (C18, C21), and thin-layer chromatography (C18) demonstrating that SAA converts large POPC MLV into small particles that are efficiently hydrolyzed by sPLA2. The controls with apoA-I/apoA-II (C20) and MLV alone (C18) strengthen the conclusion.

result: SAA enhances sPLA2-mediated hydrolysis of plasma lipoproteins (HDL and LDL) through two mechanisms: by binding to lipoproteins and remodeling them into highly curved substrates, and by augmenting sPLA2 activity even without binding to the substrate.
evaluation: Claims C22-C25 demonstrate SAA enhancement of sPLA2 activity on plasma lipoproteins through systematic experiments with HDL-bound SAA (C22), free SAA with LDL (C23), and multiple substrates (C24). The mechanistic interpretation (C25) is well-supported by the experimental data showing both binding-dependent and binding-independent effects.

result: sPLA2 hydrolysis of SAA-containing lipoproteins (but not native HDL) leads to the release of distinct 7-7.5 nm protein-containing species, regardless of the order of SAA binding and sPLA2 hydrolysis, suggesting these are stable, kinetically accessible complexes.
evaluation: Claims C26-C32 provide comprehensive evidence from non-denaturing PAGE showing that SAA-POPC particles of varying sizes (C26), SAA-HDL (C28), and SAA with hydrolyzed lipoproteins (C31) all produce 7-7.5 nm species, while native HDL does not (C27). The order-independence (C30) and requirement for both SAA and hydrolyzed phospholipids (C32) are well-documented.

result: SAA sequesters the hydrolytic products of sPLA2 (FFA and lysoPC) from diverse lipoproteins and removes them in the form of ~7 nm protein-lipid complexes containing 30-45% FFA and 12-22% PC by weight.
evaluation: Claims C33-C37 provide strong evidence from SDS PAGE, mass spectrometry (C33, C34), thin-layer chromatography (C35), and enzymatic assays (C36) characterizing the composition of the ~7 nm species. The conclusion (C37) is well-supported by the compositional data showing both proteins and lipid hydrolysis products in these complexes.

result: The ~7 nm SAA complexes formed with sPLA2 hydrolysis products are structurally distinct from both free SAA and precursor SAA-POPC particles, exhibiting ~40% α-helical structure, high thermal stability (Tm ~48°C), resistance to proteolysis, higher protein-to-lipid ratio, and more thermodynamically reversible unfolding.
evaluation: Claims C39-C47 provide comprehensive biophysical characterization using CD spectroscopy (C39-C42), thermal stability measurements (C41, C42, C47), limited proteolysis (C43), and density measurements (C46). The data consistently demonstrate that the ~7 nm complexes have distinct structural properties compared to free SAA and precursor particles, supporting the conclusion in C44.

result: SAA forms stable ~7 nm complexes with hydrolytic products from plasma LDL that exhibit similar structural properties to model SAA-POPC complexes, including ~40% α-helical structure, Tm ~45°C, thermodynamically reversible unfolding, and resistance to proteolysis.
evaluation: Claims C48-C52 demonstrate that the findings from model systems extend to plasma lipoproteins. The LDL-derived complexes contain only SAA (C48), facilitating direct comparison with model systems. CD spectroscopy (C49), thermal stability (C50), and proteolysis resistance (C51) data all support the conclusion (C52) that SAA sequesters sPLA2 products from plasma lipoproteins.

result: SAA forms stable binary complexes with individual sPLA2 products (oleic acid and lysoPC) that are structurally similar to quaternary complexes, exhibiting 35-40% α-helical structure, Tm 45-48°C, near-reversible thermal unfolding, and resistance to proteolysis.
evaluation: Claims C53-C60 demonstrate that SAA can sequester individual hydrolysis products. The data from non-denaturing PAGE (C54), CD spectroscopy (C55), thermal stability (C56, C57), and proteolysis (C58) show that binary SAA-lysoPC and SAA-OA complexes have similar properties to the quaternary complexes, supporting the conclusion (C60) that SAA can sequester lipids and their products separately or together.

result: SAA sequesters both exogenous and endogenous FFA from lipoproteins to form similar-sized ~7.5 nm complexes, as demonstrated with diabetic LDL containing 20% higher endogenous FFA than normolipidemic LDL.
evaluation: Claims C61-C63 extend the findings to physiologically relevant conditions using diabetic LDL with elevated endogenous FFA. Non-denaturing PAGE (C62) shows formation of ~7.5 nm complexes from both diabetic and normolipidemic LDL, supporting the conclusion (C63) that SAA can sequester both exogenous and endogenous FFA.

result: At physiological pH 7.5, albumin is slightly more efficient than SAA at removing FFA from LDL, but SAA's FFA removal ability remains constant across pH 4.5-7.5 while albumin's decreases at acidic pH. At acidic pH characteristic of inflammation sites, SAA removes more FFA than albumin per gram of protein.
evaluation: Claims C65-C71 provide systematic pH-dependent comparison of SAA and albumin using enzymatic FFA assays. The data clearly show albumin's pH-dependent loss of activity (C68) versus SAA's pH-independent activity (C69), with SAA being more efficient at acidic pH (C70). The conclusion (C71) about SAA's importance at inflammation sites is well-supported by the experimental data.

result: Human SAA1.1 (hSAA1.1) exhibits similar functional properties to murine SAA1.1 (mSAA1.1), forming 8.5-9 nm particles with POPC that are remodeled to ~7.5 nm upon sPLA2 hydrolysis, sequestering hydrolysis products from LDL, and removing FFA from both normolipidemic and diabetic LDL.
evaluation: Claims C72-C77 demonstrate functional conservation between human and murine SAA1.1 using non-denaturing PAGE (C72-C74) and FFA assays (C76). The parallel behavior of hSAA1.1 and mSAA1.1 across multiple assays supports the conclusion (C77) that the findings are relevant to human biology.

result: SAA and sPLA2 act synergistically to break down and remove phospholipids, with SAA enhancing sPLA2 activity by generating highly curved substrates and removing reaction products (FFA and lysophospholipids), which is important because product removal determines lipase reaction rates.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 provide a comprehensive summary of the synergistic mechanism supported by the experimental data. The dual mechanism (C80) is well-documented in the results, and the importance of product removal (C81) is supported by citation. However, C82 contains speculative elements about the 'vital role' and 'tissue healing' that extend beyond the in vitro data presented.

result: SAA can spontaneously solubilize phospholipid bilayers in an energy-independent manner to form stable nanoparticles that are hydrolyzed by sPLA2 and/or internalized by macrophages. SAA also sequesters lysoPC and FFA into stable, α-helical, proteolysis-resistant particles, augmenting sPLA2 reaction and facilitating safe removal of toxic products.
evaluation: Claims C86-C90 mix well-supported experimental findings (C87, C89 from Figures 1 and 3-5) with speculation about in vivo relevance (C86, C88, C90). The energy-independent solubilization (C87) and formation of stable complexes (C89) are experimentally demonstrated, but macrophage internalization (C88) and the proposed physiological benefits (C90) are speculative and not tested in this study.

result: SAA acts as a lipid scavenger similar to albumin but forms oligomers to sequester diverse lipophilic molecules in a hydrophobic cavity formed by amphipathic helices. SAA protects lipoproteins from oxidation by sequestering lipid hydroperoxides, and during inflammation augments albumin's action by removing FFA, lysoPC, and lipid peroxides.
evaluation: Claims C91-C96 combine prior work on SAA's antioxidant effects (C91, C92 with citations) with speculation about SAA's general role as a lipid scavenger (C93, C94). The oligomerization (C95) is supported by cross-linking data (C109), but the structural model (C96) and the proposed augmentation of albumin function (C93) are speculative extrapolations beyond the experimental data.

result: The high stability of SAA-lipid complexes contrasts with marginally stable lipid-free SAA oligomers, suggesting these oligomers are primed for lipid binding. During inflammation, albumin levels and FFA-binding capacity decrease due to post-translational modifications and acidic pH, while SAA and sPLA2 increase. SAA's superior FFA removal at acidic pH compensates for impaired albumin activity at inflammation sites, constituting a vital role in immune response.
evaluation: Claims C97-C103 combine experimental findings (C101, C102 from Figure 6) with literature citations (C99, C100) and speculation (C98, C103). The pH-dependent comparison of SAA and albumin (C101, C102) is well-supported, but the proposed 'priming' mechanism (C98) and the conclusion about SAA's 'vital role' (C103) are speculative interpretations that require in vivo validation.

result: Cross-linking experiments show that intact SAA-POPC particles contain protein monomers, dimers, and trimers, while hydrolyzed SAA-POPC particles show a prominent hexamer band, suggesting each hydrolyzed particle contains at least six SAA molecules.
evaluation: Claims C109-C110 are supported by glutaraldehyde cross-linking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D. The appearance of a hexamer band in hydrolyzed particles (C109) supports the inference that each particle contains at least six SAA molecules (C110), though the exact stoichiometry may be higher.

result: SAA is an evolutionarily conserved acute-phase protein whose plasma levels increase >1000-fold during inflammation. It is produced by the liver, binds HDL, and is secreted at inflammation sites. SAA binds diverse apolar ligands via a concave apolar face formed by amphipathic α-helices and can solubilize phospholipid vesicles to form HDL-sized particles.
evaluation: Claims C1-C10 provide well-established background information supported by multiple literature citations. These claims accurately summarize prior knowledge about SAA's evolutionary conservation (C1), acute-phase response (C2-C5), disease associations (C6, C7), ligand binding (C8-C10), and structural features (C10). All claims are appropriately referenced.

result: sPLA2 group-IIa is an antimicrobial acute-phase reactant that increases simultaneously with SAA, is co-expressed and induced by the same cytokines, and is stimulated by SAA. Clinical and in vitro studies show a link between SAA and enhanced sPLA2 activity. sPLA2 hydrolyzes highly curved surfaces like HDL but not planar bilayers.
evaluation: Claims C11-C15 provide well-documented background on sPLA2 and its relationship to SAA, supported by appropriate literature citations. These claims establish the rationale for investigating SAA-sPLA2 synergy by documenting their co-regulation (C11-C13), prior observations of their interaction (C14), and substrate preferences (C15).

result: Previous studies showed that SAA binding to POPC and other phospholipids induces α-helical folding in this intrinsically disordered protein, greatly increasing thermal stability and protecting from proteolysis.
evaluation: Claim C38 accurately summarizes prior work from the authors' laboratory and others, supported by multiple citations. This background information provides context for interpreting the structural characterization of the ~7 nm complexes in the current study.

result: In acute inflammation, plasma levels of albumin and its ability to sequester FFA and lysoPC decrease, while levels of sPLA2 and SAA increase.
evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by appropriate literature citations and provides important physiological context for understanding the potential in vivo relevance of SAA's FFA-binding activity. This establishes the rationale for comparing SAA and albumin function.

result: Unlike SAA, several other acute-phase reactants either have no effect on sPLA2 activity or inhibit it. SAA is the only acute-phase protein that enhances sPLA2 activity. The in vivo synergy between SAA and sPLA2 is probably facilitated by their simultaneous secretion systemically and locally at inflammation sites.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 are supported by literature citation (C83) and reasonable inference from the literature review (C84). Claim C85 is a reasonable speculation based on the documented co-expression and co-regulation of SAA and sPLA2, though it remains to be tested in vivo.

result: Recombinant murine SAA1.1 was expressed in E. coli and purified to 95% purity. Single-donor human lipoproteins were isolated by density gradient ultracentrifugation. SAA-HDL preparations contained varying proportions of apoA-I, apoA-II, and SAA depending on the initial SAA:apoA-I ratio.
evaluation: Claims C104-C108 describe materials and methods with appropriate citations and quantitative characterization of the SAA-HDL preparations. The protein composition data (C106-C108) are supported by SDS PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.
